name: HTML
description: Documents, landmarks, forms and the semantics that hold a page together.

lessons.title: The shape of a page
lessons.summary: Every website is one document with a head and a body. Build your first one.
objectives: Write a valid HTML document from scratch
Explain what the head and body are for
Nest elements correctly

sections.body: A page is a tree, not a pile of text

When a browser receives your HTML file it does not paint it straight away. It reads the tags and builds a **tree** in memory — the Document Object Model, or DOM. Every element you write becomes a node with a parent and children. That is why indentation matters even though the browser ignores it: the indentation is a picture of the tree you are building.

This single idea explains almost everything else in HTML. A heading inside a section is a child of that section. Two paragraphs are siblings. A tag you forget to close becomes the parent of everything after it, which is how one missing `` can wreck a whole page. Keep the tree in your head and the syntax stops feeling arbitrary.
The four parts that never change
Every valid document has the same skeleton. It looks like ceremony, but each line does a job:

sections.code:
Field notes from the coast

Three days of wind, salt and very average coffee.
sections.caption: The smallest page worth writing

items: `<!DOCTYPE html>` is not a tag with a closing partner. It switches the browser out of quirks mode and into standards mode. Omit it and the browser emulates 1999 layout bugs.
`<html>` is the root node and holds every other element. Its `lang` attribute tells screen readers which voice to use and helps search engines with language targeting.
`<head>` is metadata: information **about** the page. Nothing in it is drawn in the viewport.
`<body>` is the document itself — everything a visitor can see or interact with.
`<meta charset="UTF-8">` must come early. It tells the browser how to decode bytes into characters, so an em dash or an accent does not turn into mojibake.
`<meta name="viewport">` is what makes a page readable on a phone instead of a shrunken desktop.

sections.body: How the browser reads your file

The browser streams the file from top to bottom. When it hits `<head>` it collects metadata and starts fetching stylesheets. When it reaches `<body>` it starts building and painting the visible tree. That order is why a stylesheet in the head avoids a flash of unstyled content, and why a script at the end of the body does not block the first paint.

You never see this happen, but it explains two things you will hit soon: an element that appears before the CSS finishes loading looks unstyled for a moment, and a slow script in the head makes the whole page wait. Order in the file is order in time.
Nesting, and why closing tags matter

sections.code:
Wind from the north-east, all morning.

Wind from the north-east, all morning.
sections.caption: Elements nest, they never overlap

sections.body: Elements either sit inside one another or side by side. They never cross. When the browser meets badly overlapped tags it guesses — it will close the paragraph for you and leave the stray `` to be ignored or repaired. The page may still look fine, so the mistake survives until a later change breaks it. Browsers are forgiving; your debugging time is not.

sections.title: One stray tag breaks the tree
sections.body: If a section suddenly swallows the footer, or a paragraph turns bold halfway down the page, the cause is almost always an unclosed tag earlier in the file. Before you debug the CSS, count your opening and closing tags in that area.
Check yourself

items: What breaks if you delete `<!DOCTYPE html>`?
Which element holds the page title shown in a browser tab, and is it visible in the page itself?
Where would you put a stylesheet link, and why there?

sections.body: What to remember

items: HTML describes **what things are**, not what they look like. Styling is CSS's job.
The skeleton is fixed: doctype, `html`, `head`, `body`.
`head` is metadata, `body` is the document.
Tags nest into a tree. Close children before parents.

drills.explain: The `lang` attribute on `<html>` tells screen readers and search engines which language the page is written in. The charset meta describes encoding, not language.
hints: The attribute lives on the outermost element.

drills.prompt: Put the skeleton of a page in the order the browser reads it.
drills.explain: Doctype first, then the root element, then head and body in that order. The doctype is what puts the browser in standards mode.
hints: The head closes before the body opens.

drills.prompt: One line stops this page from being valid. Which one?
drills.explain: `<title>` is never self-closing. Without `</title>` everything after it is parsed as title text.
hints: Look for an element that opens and never closes.

lessons.title: Text that reads well
lessons.summary: Headings, paragraphs, lists and emphasis — the typography of HTML.
objectives: Use a heading hierarchy instead of bold text
Mark up lists with ul and ol
Choose strong and em for meaning, not decoration

sections.body: Two readers, one structure

Every page has at least two audiences. Sighted readers **skim** — they scan for the shape of the page before they read a word. Screen reader users often navigate by jumping between headings, never listening to the paragraphs in between. Both behaviours depend on the same thing: that your document has real structure instead of text that merely looks structured.

That is the whole argument for semantic HTML. `<h2>` is not “big bold text”. It is a declaration that a section starts here, and every tool downstream — screen readers, search engines, reader modes, browser outline views — reads that declaration.
A document with a spine

sections.code:
Brew guide

Water

Start with soft water. Hard water mutes the acidity.

Ratio

Use 60 g per litre. Adjust after the first cup, not before.

Method

  1. Rinse the filter.
  2. Bloom for 30 seconds.
  3. Pour in two stages.
sections.caption: Headings create a table of contents for free

items: `<h1>` appears once per page and names it. `<h2>` starts sections, `<h3>` subsections. Never skip a level to get a smaller font — that is a styling decision, not a structural one.

`

` is a paragraph of prose. A `
` inside a paragraph is a line break within the same thought; a new `

` is a new thought. Reach for `

` first.

`<ul>` is unordered — the order carries no meaning. `<ol>` is ordered — steps, rankings, anything where “first” matters. Screen readers announce the item numbers in an `<ol>`, which is why the recipe above is not a `<ul>`.
`<strong>` marks importance, `<em>` marks stress emphasis. Assistive technology can change its voice for both; `<b>` and `<i>` cannot communicate anything beyond looks.

sections.body: Choosing between the lookalikes

The hard part is not memorising the tags, it is picking between near-synonyms. Ask what the text **means**, not how it should look. Is this phrase important in itself? `<strong>`. Would the sentence change meaning if you stressed this word out loud? `<em>`. Is this a list of steps? `<ol>`. Is it a set of related items? `<ul>`. Is it a term and its definition? `<dl>`.

If the answer to all of those is “none of the above, I just want it bold”, the element is `<span>` and the styling belongs in CSS. A `<span>` is a neutral container: it carries no meaning, only a hook for styles.

sections.title: Do not use headings to style text
sections.body: If a line should look bold but is not a section title, use `<strong>`. If it should look big, that is CSS. Heading levels describe structure, and assistive technology builds its navigation menu from them — a fake heading sends people to the wrong place.
Check yourself

items: You need a shopping list and a recipe. Which one is `<ul>` and which is `<ol>`, and why?
Why is `<h3>` immediately after `<h1>` a problem even if it looks right?
When is `<b>` acceptable?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Structure first, appearance later.
One `h1`, then levels in order.
`ul` for sets, `ol` for sequences, `dl` for term and definition.
`strong` and `em` carry meaning; `b` and `i` only carry paint.

drills.explain: Heading elements are numbered `h1` to `h6`. An `h1` names the page; `h2` starts a section inside it.
hints: The closing tag matches the opening one exactly.

drills.prompt: Which element should wrap a list where order matters?
drills.explain: `<ol>` is an ordered list: the browser numbers the items for you. Use `<ul>` when the sequence carries no meaning.

drills.prompt: Which element gives a paragraph of text?
drills.explain:
`

` is the paragraph element. Browsers add spacing around it by default, which is why it reads as a block of prose.
hints: It is the shortest block element you know.

lessons.title: Links and images
lessons.summary: The two elements that turn a document into the web.
objectives: Write relative and absolute links
Explain what the alt attribute is for
Group navigation links in a nav element

sections.body: The two elements that make it the web

A document with no links is a dead end, and a page with no images is a wall of text. `` and `` are small elements with a large share of the accessibility surface of your site, because both depend on a human-written description that no tool can invent for you.
Links: where does this go, and what happens to the reader?

sections.code: Lessons Pricing on this page Email us MDN
sections.caption: Four links, four different kinds of destination

items: `href` takes a full URL, a site path (`/learn`), a fragment (`#pricing`), or a scheme like `mailto:` and `tel:`.
Link text is read out of context. A screen reader can list every link on the page, so “Read the CSS guide” works and “click here” becomes a list of identical anonymous items.
`target="_blank"` opens a new tab. Pair it with `rel="noreferrer"` so the new page cannot reach back through `window.opener`.
A link goes somewhere. A button does something. If it changes the page without navigating, it is a `<button>`.

sections.body: Paths, relative to what?

Relative paths are resolved against the document that contains them, not against your project folder. `coast.jpg` looks in the same directory as the current file, `/coast.jpg` starts from the site root, and `../coast.jpg` climbs one directory first. This is why a page that works at `/learn/html` can break at `/learn/html/css` — the same relative path now points somewhere else.
When in doubt, prefer root-relative paths (`/img/coast.jpg`) for assets that live in fixed places. They behave identically at every depth.
Images: the alt attribute is the image for some people

sections.caption: Two images, two different jobs

items: `alt` is what a screen reader announces and what appears if the file fails to load. Describe what the image shows and why it matters here.
Decorative images take `alt=""` — an empty string tells assistive technology to skip it. Omitting `alt` entirely makes some readers announce the filename instead.
`width` and `height` let the browser reserve space before the bytes arrive, which stops the page jumping as images load.
`loading="lazy"` defers off-screen images. Do not use it on the hero image; it delays the thing people came to see.

sections.title: Alt text is a caption, not a filename
sections.body: “Fog rolling over a grey beach at dawn” is alt text. “coast.jpg” and “image” are not. If the picture is a chart, the alt text should state the finding, not the chart type.
Check yourself

items: Why does `/learn` behave the same from any page but `learn` does not?
When is `alt=""` correct?
You have a link that opens a modal. What is wrong with it?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Links navigate; buttons act.
Root-relative paths are stable at any depth.
Every `` needs an `alt` — descriptive, or empty if decorative.
Open in a new tab deliberately, with `rel="noreferrer"`.

drills.prompt: Give the image a text alternative.
drills.explain: `alt` is what a screen reader announces and what shows if the image fails. Decorative images take `alt=""`.

drills.prompt: Which line links to a page that will not load?
drills.explain: `hraf` is a typo. The attribute is `href`, so the browser treats the second link as having no destination.
hints: Read the attribute names character by character.

drills.prompt: Which attribute holds a link's destination?
drills.explain: `href` is the hypertext reference: the URL the link points at. `src` is for embedded resources like images and scripts.

lessons.title: Semantic structure
lessons.summary: Landmarks that make a page navigable for humans, screen readers and search engines.
objectives: Replace generic divs with landmark elements
Understand header, main, section, article, footer
Keep exactly one main per page

sections.body: Divs work until someone needs to navigate

A page built from `<div class="header">` and `<div class="nav">` looks identical to one built from real landmarks. The difference appears the moment a screen reader user opens the landmarks list, or a search engine decides which part of the page is the actual content. Class names mean nothing to those tools. Element names do.
The landmarks, one by one

sections.code:
Zuno
Learn Playground

Field notes

Tide tables

...

© 2026 Zuno
sections.caption: A page skeleton made of landmarks

items: `<header>` introduces its nearest sectioning parent — the page, or a single article. A blog post can have its own header.
`<nav>` wraps a group of **major** navigation links. A list of tags in a footer does not need one.
`<main>` holds the content unique to this page. Exactly one per document, and it must not be nested inside an article or section.
`<article>` is a self-contained unit that would still make sense syndicated on its own: a post, a comment, a product card.
`<section>` groups related content, and in practice should start with a heading. A section without a heading is usually just a `<div>`.
`<footer>` closes its parent with metadata: copyright, author, related links.

sections.body: Choosing article or section

The test is portability. If you could copy this block onto another page and it would still make complete sense, it is an `<article>`. If it only makes sense as part of this page, it is a `<section>`. If it is a pure styling wrapper with no meaning at all, it is a `<div>` — and that is fine, as long as it is a deliberate choice rather than a reflex.
Headings are what make either element useful. A `<section>` with no `<h2>` gives assistive technology nothing to announce, and readers nothing to skim. Structure and labels travel together.

sections.title: Landmarks replace ARIA
sections.body: A `<nav>` already exposes `role="navigation"`. Writing both is noise. Native elements first; ARIA only when no native element fits the job.
The skip link

With landmarks in place, add one small affordance: a link at the top of the body that jumps straight to `<main>`. It is the first thing a keyboard user meets, it is usually hidden until focused, and it saves them tabbing through the entire navigation on every page.

items: Landmarks are the page's table of contents for assistive technology.

Article is portable; section is contextual; div is styling only.

lessons.title: Forms people can finish
lessons.summary: Labels, input types and validation that work before JavaScript exists.
objectives: Connect every input to a label
Pick input types that unlock the right keyboard
Use native validation before writing any JavaScript

sections.body: Forms are a conversation with a stranger

Everything else on a page is you talking. A form is the one place a visitor talks back, and the cost of a bad one is measured in abandoned signups. Almost all form pain is self-inflicted: a missing label, `type="text"` on an email field, a submit handler that fights the browser instead of using it.
The mental model: the browser already knows how to validate, focus, autofill and submit. Your job is to describe the fields accurately enough that it can help. JavaScript comes last, not first.
A form that works without JavaScript

sections.code:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required />

  <label for="password">Password</label>
  <input
    id="password"
    name="password"
    type="password"
    autocomplete="new-password"
    minlength="8"
    required
  />

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>
sections.caption: Labels, types, names and native validation

items: `<label for>` must match the input's `id`. Clicking the label then focuses the field, and screen readers announce the two together.
`type` is behaviour, not decoration: `email` gives you an `@` keyboard and a validation rule, `password` masks input, `number` gives a numeric keypad, `date` opens a picker.
`required`, `minlength`, `pattern` and `min` are enforced by the browser before submission, with messages translated into the user's language.
`name` is the key sent to the server. An input without `name` is invisible to the request.
`autocomplete` is what lets password managers and browsers fill fields correctly — `email`, `current-password`, `new-password`, `cc-number`.

sections.body: Grouping choices

Radios and checkboxes are a different problem: one label per option does not explain what the group is asking. `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` gives the group a name that assistive technology announces before the first option — “Delivery speed, three options, Standard, Express…”.

sections.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery speed</legend>

  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="standard" checked /> Standard, 3 days</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="express" /> Express, tomorrow</label>
</fieldset>
sections.caption: fieldset names the question, labels name the answers

sections.title: Placeholder is not a label
sections.body: Placeholders vanish the moment someone types, have poor contrast, and are skipped by some screen readers. Use a real `<label>`; keep the placeholder as a short hint at most, never as the only description of the field.
Errors people can act on

When validation fails, say what is wrong and how to fix it, next to the field, in plain words. “Enter an email address, for example name@example.com” beats “Invalid input”. Tie the message to the field with `aria-describedby` so it is announced when the field receives focus.
Check yourself

items: Why does an input need both `id` and `name`?
Which attribute gets you the right keyboard on a phone?
What does `<fieldset>` add that a `<div>` cannot?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Label every control, and connect it with `for`/`id`.
Pick the input type that describes the data.
Validate natively first, enhance with JavaScript second.
Group related choices with `fieldset` and `legend`.

hints: The first one names the kind of control.
The second is a boolean attribute.

options: It ties the label to the control so clicking it focuses the field
drills.explain: `for` matches the input's `id`, so the two are announced together and clicking the label focuses the field.
hints: Think about what a screen reader says.
It is about association, not looks.

lessons.title: Tables and data
lessons.summary: Real tabular data, with headers that announce themselves.
objectives: Separate structure into thead, tbody and tfoot
Use scope to bind headers to cells
Never use a table for layout

sections.body: Tables are for data with rows and columns

Tables have a bad reputation because they were abused for layout for a decade. Used correctly they are precise and irreplaceable: when information genuinely has two axes, nothing else communicates it as clearly. When it does not, a table makes the content harder for everyone.
Anatomy of a data table

sections.code:
Plan comparison
Feature Free Pro
Lessons 21 All tracks
sections.caption: Headers, a caption and scoped cells

items:
`` names the table and is announced first. It is not a heading — do not fake it with a `

` above the table.
`<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>` group rows by role. Browsers keep the header visible while scrolling and assistive technology can treat the groups separately.

`<th scope="col">` says “this header labels the column below it”. `scope="row"` says “this header labels the row beside it”. Without scope, a screen reader has to guess which header belongs to which cell.
`<td>` is data. `<th>` is a header. The difference is announced, not just bolded.

sections.body: Reading a table out loud

Imagine announcing one cell with no visual context: “Pro, 12 euros”. A screen reader does exactly that, using the row and column headers bound by `scope`. If your headers are `<td>` elements styled bold, the announcement becomes “12 euros” and the number loses its meaning.
This is also the test for whether you need a table at all. If you cannot name the rows and the columns, you have a list or a grid of cards, not a table.

sections.title: Tables are not layouts
sections.body: Using a table to place a sidebar was normal in 2004. Today it breaks responsiveness, and screen readers announce a data grid that does not exist. Use CSS grid or flexbox.
Small screens

Tables have a minimum width; text does not. On narrow screens, wrap the table in a container with `overflow-x: auto` so it scrolls sideways instead of squeezing columns into unreadable slivers. If a table needs more than a scroll to work on a phone, it probably wants to become a list of cards at that breakpoint.
Check yourself

items: Why does `scope` matter if the headers are already bold?
When does a table stop being the right element?
What is announced first when a screen reader reaches a table?

sections.body: What to remember

items: Only real tabular data goes in a table.
`caption` names it, `thead`/`tbody` structure it.
`th` plus `scope` is what makes a cell understandable on its own.
Wrap wide tables in a scroll container.

drills.explain: Head, body, rows, cells. `scope="col"` tells assistive tech that the header describes the column below it.

drills.prompt: Which element marks a header cell in a table?

lessons.title: Media, metadata and accessible widgets
lessons.summary: Figures, disclosure widgets and the tags search engines and screen readers read first.
objectives: Pair media with captions using figure and figcaption
Use details and summary instead of a JS accordion
Give icon-only buttons an accessible name

sections.body: The details that separate working from pleasant

By now the page has structure, text, links, landmarks and a form. The last layer is the small set of elements that make a page feel finished: captioned media, native disclosure widgets, icon buttons that have a name, and metadata that search engines and social previews read before a human ever arrives.
Media with a caption that belongs to it

sections.caption: figure binds the caption to the media

sections.body: `<figure>` is any self-contained unit — an image, a code sample, a chart, a quote — with an optional `<figcaption>`. The caption must be the first or last child, and it is announced as part of the figure rather than as a stray paragraph after it. The `alt` describes the image; the caption adds context. They are not duplicates.
Disclosure without JavaScript

sections.code:
What happens after the trial ends?

Your progress stays. Lessons lock until you pick a plan.
sections.caption: details and summary: keyboard support included

sections.body: `<details>` is a native accordion. It opens with Enter or Space, exposes its expanded state to assistive technology, works with find-in-page, and needs zero JavaScript. A hand-rolled version reproduces all of that badly, then breaks when someone tabs into it.
Buttons that only contain an icon

An icon button has no text for a screen reader to announce, so it needs a name from somewhere. `aria-label` supplies it. The SVG inside should be `aria-hidden="true"` so the reader does not try to describe paths and shapes. And it must be a `<button>`, not a clickable `<div>` — a div is not focusable and does not respond to Enter.

sections.code:
<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" viewBox="0 0 16 16">
    <path d="M4 4l8 8M12 4l-8 8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" />
  </svg>
</button>
sections.caption: A name for the reader, pixels for the eye

sections.body: Metadata people never see but search engines do

`<title>` is the clickable headline in search results and the label on a browser tab. `<meta name="description">` is the snippet underneath, usually truncated around 155 characters. Both should describe this specific page — a site-wide description is worse than none. `og:title` and `og:image` control what appears when the link is shared in a chat app.

sections.title: Test with the Tab key
sections.body: Everything interactive must be reachable with Tab and operable with Enter or Space. If you cannot do it without a mouse, neither can a lot of your visitors — and it takes thirty seconds to check.

drills.prompt: A decorative background image should have which alt text?
drills.explain: An empty `alt` marks the image as decorative, so screen readers skip it. Leaving the attribute out makes some readers announce the file name instead.
